speaker: Will Guidara
title: Talking Unreasonable Hospitality, Culture, and Leadership with Will Guidara
question: In high-touch hospitality and retail, why does jumping straight into casual familiarity with a new customer often fail to build genuine rapport?
guest: We used to say this all the time, and I think it's actually a great thing for anyone in any business to use. We would talk about earning informality. The job of our team was to earn informality with everyone we served. And what that meant was two things. One, you begin the relationship on a foundation of formality. The example I use is when I met my wife's dad, before she was my wife, I called him Mr. Tosi, right? But my entire job in relationship with him was to get to the point where he said, "Hey, Will, call me Gino." Now, if I had called him Gino the first time we met, I guarantee you she would not be my wife right now. So you start off on a relationship of formality. You need to earn the right to be informal, and also, you better earn it, because genuine relationship does not exist on a foundation of formality. You need to get people to let you in, and that can happen through eye contact. It can happen through humor. It can happen through consistency. It can happen through vulnerability.

points.core: Premature informality before establishing trust violates baseline respect with new customers.
points.note: Accept: starting on a foundation of formality is required because skipping respect alienates customers upfront. Do not credit: generic advice to be polite or professional.

points.core: Staying permanently formal prevents genuine human connection from forming with customers.
points.note: Accept: real relationships cannot develop on formality alone, so staff must eventually move past rigid etiquette. Do not credit: claiming casual service is always superior to formal service.

points.core: Staff must deliberately earn customer warmth through consistent small signals of humanity.
points.note: Accept: winning permission to become informal via eye contact, humor, consistency, or personal vulnerability. Do not credit: scripted friendliness or generic small talk from the start.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because familiarity is something a customer grants, not something staff can claim. Real rapport rests on trust, and trust is built by first showing competence, attentiveness, and respect. When an employee opens with instant chumminess—first names, jokes, personal questions, a buddy-buddy tone—they are acting out a relationship that doesn't yet exist. Customers tend to read this as scripted, presumptuous, or a sales tactic, which triggers guardedness rather than warmth.

It also skips the most important step: reading the person. In high-touch settings, guests vary widely in how much interaction they want, and their expectations are shaped by culture, age, mood, and occasion. Unearned informality imposes the employee's preferred style instead of adapting to the customer's, signaling that the interaction is about the staff member rather than the guest. It can also undermine the sense of professionalism and status that premium customers are paying for.

The more reliable path is to start with polished, attentive formality, pick up on the customer's cues, and let them set the level of closeness. Warmth that follows their lead feels personal; warmth that precedes it feels performed.

In high-touch hospitality and retail, genuine rapport depends on earned trust and emotional attunement, both of which premature familiarity undermines. Jumping straight into a casual, overly friendly tone assumes an intimacy that has not yet been invited, crossing subtle boundaries of status, privacy, and cultural expectation. Because elevated service promises individualized care, leading with an instant "old friend" persona signals the opposite: that the associate is running a generic script or centering their own style rather than reading the individual in front of them.

Different guests arrive wanting very different interactions—some welcome conversation, while others seek quiet discretion or crisp efficiency—and unsolicited informality pressures them to reciprocate socially instead of feeling at ease. Discerning customers also tend to recognize unearned closeness as a performative, transactional sales tactic, which triggers guardedness rather than trust. Lasting rapport in high-touch environments starts with warm, poised professionalism—establishing respect and competence first—and allows the customer's own cues and comfort level to set the pace toward familiarity.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Instant familiarity fails because rapport is earned over time, and acting as if it already exists skips the step where trust gets built. A first-name greeting, a joke, or a "hey buddy" tells a new guest you're claiming closeness you haven't earned. Many people read that as presumptuous, scripted, or manipulative, especially in luxury settings, where they expect to be respected and treated with some ceremony.

It also hides the most important thing at the start: reading the person. Customers want different things. Some want warmth and chat, others want quiet efficiency, privacy, or formality, and that can depend on culture, age, mood, or why they're there. If you open casually, you're assuming their preference instead of noticing it.

Good service tends to start polite and attentive, then follows the guest's cues and warms up step by step. Remembering a preference, showing real interest, and letting the customer set the pace makes them feel seen. Unearned informality has the opposite effect: they feel like a generic target of a sales technique. Rapport is something the two of you build together over time, and an opening line can't create it.

In high-touch hospitality and retail, genuine rapport depends on earned trust and psychological safety, not instant closeness. When staff jump straight into casual familiarity with a new customer, they bypass the foundational step of establishing respect, competence, and clear boundaries. Because no real relationship exists yet, premature informality often feels presumptuous or performative—more like a scripted sales tactic than authentic warmth—which triggers skepticism rather than comfort.

It also takes away the customer's agency to set the social distance. Guests and shoppers arrive with different moods, expectations, and cultural norms; what feels friendly to one person can feel intrusive or unprofessional to another. Leading with poised, attentive professionalism creates a respectful baseline that makes the customer feel cared for without pressure. From there, staff can read the customer's cues and mirror their level of openness, allowing warmth to develop organically as a response to the individual rather than an assumption imposed on them.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Casual familiarity assumes a level of trust that a new customer hasn’t had time to develop. First-name banter, teasing, or personal questions can land well with a regular. With someone you’ve just met, they can feel scripted or intrusive and put the customer in the awkward position of having to play along.

Genuine rapport grows when the customer feels understood and can set the pace. A warm greeting, attentive listening, and a helpful response to what they actually need give them a reason to relax. As they signal that they’re comfortable with a more casual tone, the interaction can become more personal naturally.

Jumping straight into casual familiarity assumes a level of trust the customer hasn’t had a chance to develop. A joke or nickname that makes a regular feel recognized can make a newcomer feel obliged to play along, especially if they wanted privacy or just needed help.

Warmth can start immediately. Familiarity works best when it grows out of the interaction. A courteous welcome, room to browse, or a well-chosen question shows that the employee is paying attention. If the customer then lingers to chat or jokes back, a more casual tone feels mutual. That responsiveness is what builds rapport.
